title: Placebo works even when you know it is one
_format: 1080x1350 = 4:5. NICHT 3:4 — die Instagram-API akzeptiert beim automatischen Veroeffentlichen nur 4:5 bis 1.91:1. Bildprompts bleiben 3:4, ihre schwarze Fusszone faengt die Differenz ab.
_syntax: [Klammern] = Akzentfarbe mit Textur (nur in headline). **Sterne** = fett in bullets/body. Zeilenumbruch = eigener Array-Eintrag. `alt` pro Slide ist Pflicht — Buffer verlangt altText beim Upload.

caption.kern: Patients were handed a bottle labelled placebo pills and told plainly there was no active ingredient in it. They got better anyway. 💊🤯
caption.detail: Ted Kaptchuk's team at Harvard Medical School randomised 80 people with irritable bowel syndrome. One group got open-label placebos plus the usual care. The other got the usual care and the same amount of attention from the same clinicians. On the IBS Global Improvement Scale at day 21, the placebo group scored 5.0 against 3.9.
caption.kontext: Nobody was deceived. That is the part that broke the textbook: the placebo effect was supposed to need a lie to work. It doesn't. What it seems to need is the ritual — a diagnosis, a bottle, a routine, and someone who takes you seriously.
caption.frage: Would you take a pill you know is empty, if it worked?
caption.sources: Sources: Kaptchuk, Friedlander, Kelley, Sanchez, Kokkotou, Singer, Kowalczykowski, Miller, Kirsch & Lembo — Placebos without deception: a randomized controlled trial in irritable bowel syndrome • PLoS ONE 5(12): e15591, December 2010 • doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0015591
